key_facts: Under Japanese government guidelines issued in 2021, estate agents must disclose suicide, murder, death by fire, and deaths where the body was not discovered for an extended period; for rentals this must be disclosed for three years, and indefinitely for properties offered for sale.
Tenant Ryua rents a 25 sq m bedsit in Setagaya, Tokyo, for 45,000 yen ($285; £213) a month instead of 62,000 yen, an almost 30% discount, after being told a man had killed himself in the apartment.
In Kagoshima, Diane Tincher bought a three-bedroom house for 20m yen where similar properties usually sell for up to 45m yen, after an elderly woman died alone there.

Oshimaland, a crowdsourced website launched in 2005 in Tokyo and expanded nationally and internationally in 2011, lists 'jiko bukken' (stigmatised/incident properties); a 2025 survey found more than half of Japanese respondents would rent such a property if it was cheap.
importance_reason: Feature-style human-interest piece about niche real estate practices; no direct market or macro impact.
